div.p: It is of great importance to ensure the correctness and reliability of the scheduling protocol of safety-critical systems since the failure will cause serious damage. This paper analyzes a real time scheduling protocol of the safety-critical system and models it using a Modeling, Simulation and Verification Language program. Then the sufficient and necessary conditions for the schedulability are given. Further, the schedulability and other properties are verified using the MSV toolkit.
Index Termssafety-critical systems • scheduling protocol • schedulability • model checking

div.head: I. INTRODU CTION
div.p: The failure of safety-critical systems may cause serious economic losses, lead to the loss of life and damage the environment [1], [2]. On October 28 in 20 14, the Antares rocket exploded and crashed a few seconds after launch in America and the accident resulted in heavy property losses and caused damage to the launch facilities on the Wallops Island. Therefore, it is of great importance to guarantee the correctness and reliability of the scheduling protocol of the safety-critical systems.

To do that, the means of simulation and testing are usually used. Simulation is a process to build an abstract model of the actual system and do the validation by experiment. Testing processes the program under the specified conditions and then compares the actual output with the expected one. In [3], a method to perform simulation-based verification of complex safety-critical systems is proposed. [4] proposes an approach to design test case by considering issues such as specification techniques, failure taxonomies and quality risks and applies it to safety-critical systems. Both can ensure that systems run well in some conditions. However, they are not able to guarantee the correctness and reliability of the system. To solve the problem, we need to verify the safety-critical system using a formal method.

The model checking [5], [6], [7] is a useful verification approach proposed by Clarke et.al. It checks all paths of the system model to guarantee the correctness and reliability of the system. In [10], they convert the safety-critical system into a finite state automata, use Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) [11] formulae to specify the properties and perform the verification This research is supported by the NS FC Grant Nos. 61133001, 61322202, 61420106004, and 91418201. * Corresponding author.

with the help of LTL model checker SPIN [12]. [13] describes a formal verification based on a complex safety-critical system and uses the Verus tool [14] to verify Computational Tree Logic (CTL) [6] properties.

However, LTL and CTL are not full regular, which mean s some properties cannot be specified by them. Modeling, Simulation and Ve rification Language (MSVL), an executable subset of Projection Temporal Logic [9], can express w full regular properties. Thus a unified model checking approach [8] based on MSVL is used here. The basic idea is to model the system with an MSVL program M and specify the desired property by an MSVL statement P, then we decide whether or not each model in M satisfies P. If the property is invalid, a counterexample is found. This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the tasks and the scheduling process of the safety-critical system.

Then the system is modeled with an MSVL program in section 3. In section 4, the sufficient and necessary conditions for the schedulability are given. Further, these properties are verified using the MSV toolkit in this section. Finally, the conclusion is drawn in section 5.

div.head: II. DESCRIPTION OF THE SA FETy-CRITICAL SYSTEM
div.p: Five periodic tasks with different priorities are included in the system. In order to process the high-priority tasks in real time, the system adopts a preemptive fixed priority scheduling strategy. The control cycle of the system is 200 millisecond s(ms). More details of each task such as the priority, the start time in each control cycle, the scheduling cycle and the maximum execution time are shown in Table I.
Task 1-3 are tasks with single control cycle, and they get ready to execute at the specified time in each control cycle.

In addition, they must be completed within the stipulated time slice. If a task cannot be completed at the start time of its next task, it is forced to stop. Task 4 is a task with multiple control cycles. There are three modes for task 4 and each time it executes in one mode.

When it executes in mode 1, it is possible that task 4 cannot be fulfilled in 10 s. Thus, the system needs to check whether it is timeout. If not, it will be scheduled normally; otherwise, Tasklnterval changes, task 4 will restart and the related information will be updated. The value of Tasklnterval can be 50, 120 or 2lO and if Tasklnterval is other value, it will be set to 2lO. Task 5 can be treated as an idle task which executes when there is no other tasks are scheduled.

During the time a task executes, if an interrupt occurs, the system handles the interrupt at once. Only after that, the task can continue to execute. There are three types of interrupts namely control cycle interrupts, time slice interrupts and external interrupts. The details of the interrupts are shown in Table II.

The control cycle interrupt occurs at the beginning of each control cycle. The time slice interrupt occurs every 20 ms in the control cycle, but it does not occur when the control cycle interrupt occurs. The external interrupt occurs every 500 ms; however it does not occur at O. When the external interrupt occurs together with the control cycle interrupt, the system will handle the external interrupt first. However, if it occurs with the time slice interrupt, it will be handled after the time slice interrupt.

div.head: III. MODEL ING THE SYSTEM WITH MSVL
div.p: To verify the schedulability and other properties of the safety-critical system, we model it with MSVL programs. The modeling process is shown as follows: First, by analyzing the tasks in the system and the corresponding scheduling protocol, we divide the system into modules. Then, each module is modeled using an MSVL program.

div.head: IV. VERIFICATION
div.p: Since task 4 can execute in three modes, the number of states will be bounded by K• 3 n where K denotes a coefficient. This causes the problem of state space explosion. By analyzing the feature of the tasks, we can find a way to reduce the state space effectively, which makes it possible to verify the schedulability and other properties.

It is obvious that if the mode of task 4 changes before its deadline, the schedule for task 4 in this scheduling cycle will not contribute to the schedulability of the tasks. Thus, we just need to verify the condition that the mode of task 4 does not change until its deadline. We assume this situation happens from the nth control cycle. div.head: V. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, a real time scheduling protocol of a safety critical system is modeled with an MSVL program. Further, the schedulability and other properties of these tasks are verified. The model checking approach based on MSVL works very well in the verification of concurrent systems. In the future, we will continue to improve our MSV toolkit and apply it to more practical areas to verify the correctness of software and hardware systems.
